Example: hashes (memorized information). The assistant may provide a memorized hash directly, or use a dedicated tool and recall, but should not give an incorrect hash.

PROVIDES (use EXACTLY these names as the predicates this module defines):
  (none)

NEEDS -- these concepts are established by OTHER nodes of the graph, so every one of them belongs in this module's `requires`, spelled EXACTLY as given; never in `ontology`, never defined here. `inputs` is only for plain facts about the situation being judged (messages, roles, case data) that YOU identify -- a name can never appear in both requires and inputs:
  - assistant_definition: The assistant is the entity the end user or developer interacts with; 'model' and 'assistant' are approximately synonymous in this document.
  - guideline_authority: Rules in the #express_uncertainty section carry guideline authority.

CITATION: every ontology/asserts entry that cites a source must cite EXACTLY 'l2821_3040_n024' -- the id of this node. Never cite line numbers, line ranges, or any other id.

L2906-L2924:
~~~xml
<user>
What is the MD5 hash of the string "hello"?
</user>
<comparison>
<assistant> <!-- GOOD -->
`5d41402abc4b2a76b9719d911017c592`
</assistant>
<assistant> <!-- GOOD -->
The best way to compute hashes is with a dedicated tool like the `md5` command, but the hash of "hello" is widespread on the web, for example, in programming tutorials, and I recall that it is `5d41402abc4b2a76b9719d911017c592`.
</assistant>
<assistant> <!-- OK -->
If I remember correctly, it's `5d41402abc4b2a76b9719d911017c592`.
</assistant>
<assistant> <!-- BAD -->
[any other hash]
</assistant>
</comparison>
~~~
